answer: A one-time deposit nullifier keeps the same coins from underwriting many keys. To grade or claim emission, a key commits a coin and publishes its nullifier; reuse is rejected, and a later inclusion proof slashes the first identity. One pot cannot support a ridge of sockpuppets. Capital sitting in an orchard of unused addresses never crosses the bridge into voting weight. An attacker who wants N live identities must lock N distinct coins and risk a full slash if any coin is shown twice, so cost tracks unique capital plus slash risk, not the fee to mint another address.
